title: CVE-2025-0725: gzip integer overflow
final_label: Real behavior, maybe not a security issue
explain: The code does what the report says, but curl's own policy may exclude it. A maintainer decides.
receipts_override: the behavior is real; the project's policy section 'Not practically possible' may exclude it
summary: The report claims that libcurl's gzip handling in content_encoding.c has an integer overflow leading to heap corruption and arbitrary free() of attacker-controlled data when Content-Encoding: gzip is used.

claims.text: integer overflow of z->avail_in in line 533
claims.reasoning: The code adds nbytes to z->avail_in without any bounds check. Since z->avail_in is a 32-bit unsigned integer (uInt) and nbytes is size_t (64-bit on modern systems), repeated additions can wrap around.

citations.note: z->avail_in += (uInt) nbytes; with no overflow check; z->avail_in is uInt (32-bit), nbytes is size_t

claims.text: Curl_saferealloc() called with overflowed size causing shrink of z->next_in
claims.reasoning: If z->avail_in has overflowed to a small value, Curl_saferealloc will shrink the allocation to that small size.

citations.note: z->next_in = Curl_saferealloc(z->next_in, z->avail_in); called with potentially wrapped-around size

claims.text: memcpy() writes out-of-bounds before z->next_in after shrink
claims.reasoning: After overflow, z->avail_in is small while nbytes is large. The expression z->avail_in - nbytes underflows in unsigned arithmetic, producing a huge positive offset that writes far before the buffer start.

citations.note: memcpy(z->next_in + z->avail_in - nbytes, buf, nbytes); with small z->avail_in and large nbytes causes unsigned wraparound

claims.text: free(z->next_in) puts forged chunk into allocator freelist
claims.reasoning: When check_gzip_header returns GZIP_OK, the code frees z->next_in which now points to a heap chunk with corrupted metadata due to the preceding OOB write.

citations.note: free(z->next_in); frees the corrupted pointer after the OOB write

claims.text: z->avail_in can be repeatedly incremented by attacker data causing endless calls to gzip_do_write()
claims.reasoning: When check_gzip_header returns GZIP_UNDERFLOW (e.g., waiting for NUL-terminated filename), the function returns success and remains in ZLIB_GZIP_HEADER state, allowing the attacker to send unlimited data that increments z->avail_in each time.

citations.note: case GZIP_UNDERFLOW: return CURLE_OK; keeps state as ZLIB_GZIP_HEADER for more data
Each call adds nbytes to z->avail_in

claims.text: attacker can trigger integer overflow of z->avail_in with endlessly large gzip headers
claims.reasoning: By setting the ORIG_NAME flag (flag 8) and sending a very long filename without a NUL terminator, check_gzip_header returns GZIP_UNDERFLOW repeatedly, keeping the parser in ZLIB_GZIP_HEADER state and allowing unlimited growth of z->avail_in until overflow.

citations.note: if(flags & ORIG_NAME) { while(len && *data) { --len; ++data; } if(!len || *data) return GZIP_UNDERFLOW; }

key_reasons: All six claims are technically correct for the code path under #ifdef OLD_ZLIB_SUPPORT
However, this code is only compiled when OLD_ZLIB_SUPPORT is defined, which supports zlib versions < 1.2.0.4 (released 2003)
The comment at line 474-476 states 'Support for old zlib versions is compiled away' when OLD_ZLIB_SUPPORT is not defined, indicating the default build excludes this path
No modern system uses zlib that old; the feature is effectively obsolete and not enabled in standard installations
Per project policy 'Not practically possible: If the flaw or vulnerability cannot practically get executed on existing hardware it is not a security problem'
missing_info: Build configuration default for OLD_ZLIB_SUPPORT (not provided in sources)
reply: Thank you for the detailed report. The code you cite does contain the integer overflow and subsequent heap corruption you describe, but only in the code path guarded by #ifdef OLD_ZLIB_SUPPORT. This path exists solely to support zlib versions older than 1.2.0.4 (from 2003). In default builds this code is compiled away (see lines 473-476), and no modern system runs such an ancient zlib. Per our policy, vulnerabilities that cannot practically be executed on existing hardware — including those in obsolete, off-by-default compatibility layers — are not considered security issues. If you have evidence that OLD_ZLIB_SUPPORT is enabled by default in common distributions, please share it.
